maintopic: THE LATE WILLIAM L. HOUCK TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR NIAGARA FALLS

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE LATE WILLIAM L. HOUCK TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR NIAGARA FALLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all hon. members of this house have been deeply saddened by the news that since we rose last evening death has claimed one of the members of this house, namely William Limburg Houck, the late member for Niagara Falls.
Every one of us recognizes that in the death of Mr. Houck this country has lost a devoted public servant who in his service in this chamber was always animated by the highest purposes. He entered this chamber in 1953 and was re-elected at the general elections of 1957 and 1958. It is no exaggeration to say that he was one of the most popular and most respected members of this house. This parliament is much the poorer for his passing.
The country has likewise suffered a loss in other respects. The late Mr. Houck was not bom in Canada. He had come to this country from the United States. He was educated in that country, and was a graduate of Cornell. He settled in the city of Niagara Falls and over the years had rendered distinguished service not only in his community but in the province of his adoption. He was elected to the Ontario legislature for that riding in 1934 and served as an elected member in the legislature until 1943. From 1937 to 1943 he was a minister without portfolio in the Ontario government and vice-chairman of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario.
In his community also he enlarged his service in the years from 1947 to 1950 when he served as mayor of the city of Niagara Falls. His community, the province, the country and this parliament have suffered a loss that all of us will feel very keenly.
May I be forgiven one personal remark, Mr. Speaker. I had known Mr. Houck personally for many years, and I think I can say that there existed between us a bond of warm, personal friendship. I am sure there are many other hon. members who had
the same warm, personal feeling toward Mr. Houck and who had enjoyed something of the warmth of his friendship and his delightful personal attributes, including his ever-manifest kindness. All of us in that respect are conscious of our personal loss.
On behalf of the government, Mr. Speaker, I extend to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) our special condolences on the loss he has suffered, and I doubt not that I speak for all hon. members of this house, indeed for the Canadian people, in extending to the widow and daughter of our late and highly esteemed member our sincere sympathy in the crushing loss which has fallen upon them.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE WILLIAM L. HOUCK TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR NIAGARA FALLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members of our party and on my own behalf I would like to thank the Acting Prime Minister for what he has said, and to express to him our appreciation of the way he has said it.
Our hearts, Mr. Speaker, are heavy and sad on this bright and sunny spring day because we have all lost a very dear friend. As the Acting Prime Minister has said, Bill Houck was a man whose whole adult life was spent in public service to his city; and we in the house remember how he loved his city, Niagara Falls, and how impossible it was for him to make a speech in this house on any subject without bringing Niagara Falls into it. He devoted himself to his city, to his province and to his country; not the country of his birth, as the Acting Prime Minister has said, but the country of his choice. He included in this service-and he himself would put it very high in service-the promotion of friendship and good neighbourliness between his two countries.
Because of his service Bill Houck was greatly admired and respected, and because of himself he was greatly loved. Few men have had more friends, and no man has deserved them more. In political life he was a loyal and devoted member of his party. You could always count on him; but he was no narrow partisan, and his friendly feelings recognized no party line. That, of course, is the way it should be. His interests were as broad and deep as his friendships, and he was always anxious to help in any good cause. He will be greatly missed for a very long time, and will not be forgotten by those who had the great privilege of his friendship.

The late W. L. Houck
Mr. Speaker, I join the Acting Prime Minister in extending to Mrs. Houck, whose quiet and deep affection and loyal and unselfish support sustained him over so many years, and to his family our most heartfelt sympathy in their great loss.

maintopic: THE LATE WILLIAM L. HOUCK TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR NIAGARA FALLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one of those sad and difficult occasions which come far too frequently to the House of Commons. We have lost a member of this house who was truly beloved by all hon. members in all parts. This man was exceedingly kind in all his relations with members of his own party and with members of other parties in this house. His was a life of unselfish and devoted service to his country, service which ranged from the municipal level as mayor of Niagara Falls and a long and distinguished service in the Ontario legislature to distinguished service over a number of years in the Canadian House of Commons.
It was my privilege-and I feel the better for it, because of my experience-to be among the delegation from this house which went to Washington last year and which included Bill Houck among its members. During that occasion we came to know one another better. We saw him during all the discussions putting forward very sincerely, very conscientiously and very ably the Canadian point of view.
We extend to Mrs. Houck, to her daughter, and to the leader and members of the Liberal party our sincere sympathy. Canada today lost a very distinguished citizen.

maintopic: THE LATE WILLIAM L. HOUCK TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR NIAGARA FALLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join our leaders in paying tribute to the memory of a deskmate, a good neighbour and a true friend.
Bill Houck gave many years of his life to public service and, as has been said, he served his area well. He served it with distinction and great ability as mayor of Niagara Falls, then as a member of the Ontario legislature and latterly as a member of this House of Commons. Because of his great interest in power development it was very natural that he should be appointed as minister to represent the hydro electric power commission in a former government of Ontario. Born in the United States and graduated from a university there, he was always very loyal to his adopted country and to bur institutions. He was possessed of those fine qualities which made him a friend to everyone.
We all deeply mourn his passing, and I join with all hon. members here in sending condolences to Mrs. Houck and her family.

maintopic: THE LATE WILLIAM L. HOUCK TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR NIAGARA FALLS
speechtext:
May I
be allowed to say a few words on this mournful occasion. I am sure it came as a shock
to everyone in this house to hear that Bill Houck had passed away early this morning. We came into the house together in 1953 and shared the same office until his recent illness.
Bill had no enemies; he was gracious, unselfish, kind, no matter whether it was in his private life or in his political life during which he gave commendable service on three levels as has been already stated. May I take this opportunity of expressing my deepest sympathy to Mrs. Houck and the family in this irreparable loss.

maintopic: THE LATE WILLIAM L. HOUCK TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR NIAGARA FALLS
speechtext: I should like very much to associate myself with those hon. members who have expressed their very deep sympathy in the loss of the late member for Niagara Falls. I had the pleasure of being associated with him over many years in the Ontario legislature and again here in the House of Commons. I can only corroborate those words which were so well spoken by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) and others as to Mr. Houck's outstanding qualities of citizenship and the efforts he put forth while serving as minister without portfolio in the Ontario legislature to co-operate with each and every member of that body.

maintopic: THE LATE WILLIAM L. HOUCK TRIBUTES TO DECEASED MEMBER FOR NIAGARA FALLS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss if at this time I did not rise on behalf of the people of my constituency to express my own personal regret and also the regret of my people at the passing of Bill Houck. Bill's riding was very close to mine. He was a very great personal friend of mine and also an active supporter of the interests of the Niagara peninsula. At this time on behalf of the people of Lincoln county I pay tribute to Mr. Houck and extend my sympathy and that of my constituents to his family and friends.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TABLING OF LETTERS RESPECTING VOLUNTARY LIMITATION OF JAPANESE EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table copies of three letters which I have today received from the ambassador of Japan informing me of certain voluntary export limitations which the Japanese government has decided to impose on shipments to Canada of textile products and stainless steel flatware during the year 1960. The letters themselves are self-explanatory. I would ask the house to give consent to have these letters printed as an appendix to Hansard, if such is the wish of hon. members for their convenience.
If I may I should like to make a few brief explanatory comments explaining the significance of these arrangements, in view of the number of questions that have been put to me in the house from time to time recently by hon. members.
The first letter sets out in detail the arrangements for 1960 in respect of textile products. I can describe these arrangements under four headings. Items 6 to 11, covering cotton fabrics and various cotton products, have been subject to Japanese export restraint for several years now, and it will be observed that for these items the arrangements generally provide for a moderate and orderly increase for the year 1960 as compared with shipments in 1959. There are several exceptions to this, and these occur in the garment items which are particularly sensitive by virtue of the flooding situation which occurred during 1959 for similar items made of spun rayon.
The second category, items 1 to 4, consists of made-up goods of spun rayon which were first brought under export control during 1959. Hon. members will recall that in these items very large increases in Japanese shipments occurred during the year 1959, which created in fact a situation of flooding. For these items the 1960 quota levels are based on the shipments during 1958, and represent a significant decrease from the excessively high levels of 1959.
The third category includes items 5, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 16, for which controls on shipments to Canada are being introduced for the first time. For these products the quota levels are based on 1959 shipments, plus an orderly increase; with the exception of
5. 1960	3571
Limitation of Japanese Exports to Canada cotton sheets, in respect of which, because of the very large increase in 1959, there will be no change from the level of that year.
The fourth category consists of other secondary textile products on which the Japanese government maintains voluntary controls. Some of these are subject to individual quota control, while others are subject to a general licensing control. The Japanese government has not indicated precise quantitative limits on the shipments of these products to Canada, but it will be observed that in the letter we have been given an undertaking that 1960 shipments will provide for moderate and orderly expansion.
I should also point out that for several categories of garments the former quota groups have been divided into subquotas in order to avoid undue concentration on particular sensitive products.
I should like to say to the house on this occasion that I share the hope expressed by the ambassador of Japan that these controls should effectively preclude any further flooding in textiles, and that Japan in taking these self-restraining measures has helped to pave the way for the further expansion of twoway trade between Canada and Japan on an orderly basis to the mutual benefit of both countries.
May I turn now to make a brief comment on the second letter, which deals with stainless steel flatware. The increases in Japanese shipments of flatware which have occurred in the past few years have been unusually large. The Japanese government has now decided to establish a voluntary control for 1960 which is substantially below the 1959 level of shipments.
The third letter is entirely self-explanatory. It simply reiterates the concern of the Japanese government that a situation should not arise in which third countries are able to expand their sales to Canada by virtue of the fact that Japan has undertaken to limit her shipments of the products concerned.
Finally, I should like to say that consultations are continuing with representatives of the Japanese government concerning the need for export restraints on other products. These include hardwood plywood, rubber-soled canvas and waterproofed footwear, plastic rainwear and several other products.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TABLING OF LETTERS RESPECTING VOLUNTARY LIMITATION OF JAPANESE EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Acting Prime Minister's announcement is a good one, dealing as it does with trade between Canada and Japan, in view of the fact that Japan is one of our largest and most important markets and becoming, we hope, larger and even more important.
3572	HOUSE OF
Limitation of Japanese Exports to Canada
In so far as steps have been taken or can be taken to protect our own producers against dumping or unfair competition, there can be no argument against those steps; but, Mr. Speaker, if the Japanese government, by actions which it terms voluntary but which are taken under pressure, adopts policies which create resentment in Japan as being unfair, then if counter action is taken in Japan we in this country would suffer a great deal more than the Japanese would suffer because of the nature of the trade.
We will study these letters. I want to make clear we are not objecting to any steps that can be taken to protect Canadian industries against unfair competition and dumping, but we have to be very careful in connection with action taken against one of our largest customers.

maintopic: TABLING OF LETTERS RESPECTING VOLUNTARY LIMITATION OF JAPANESE EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
I think the documents that have been referred to by the Acting Prime Minister demonstrate at least one point, namely that inevitably there has to be a measure of planning in respect to international trade. I thank the minister for having sent over copies of these documents, but I do regret that I received them only about midway in his own statement. It would have been much more helpful, Mr. Speaker, if it had been possible to have these documents at least some time beforehand.
We in the C.C.F. think the government's policy in regard to international trade in general should be one of expanding trade. We think that in the days ahead there must be a tremendous expansion in Canadian trade and in world trade, and we feel that the future role of Canada lies in the direction of taking steps to remove trade barriers. However, we are mindful of some of the difficulties experienced by the industries affected by importations of certain goods. We have sympathy for the workers who are on the streets, who have been displaced. We feel that action which is taken against the dumping of goods into this country is something that is necessary.
We do feel, and feel very strongly, that even with a system of planned trade there is room both for a large increase in exports and for a substantial domestic industry with full employment, which we do not now enjoy.

I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. It arises out of the letters he tabled a moment ago in connection with the quota arrangements made between Canada and Japan. As the minister read the letters two questions came to my mind. The first was this. What happens if the quota is exceeded? I understand that under an earlier arrangement, which was far more flexible than this one, the quota with regard to certain of the goods, particularly textiles, was exceeded. Thus, the question I should like to put is, what happens between the two countries if the quotas mentioned in the letter are exceeded, having regard to the item concerning textiles?
The second question is, are the dumping duties superseded by these letters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TABLING OF LETTERS RESPECTING VOLUNTARY LIMITATION OF JAPANESE EXPORTS TO CANADA
speechtext:
The answer to the first question is that if these quotas were to be exceeded the Canadian government would be entirely free at any time to invoke those provisions of the 1954 treaty of commerce between Canada and Japan under which the Canadian government possesses the right to apply special valuations for duty purposes on imports from Japan. The hon. member will recall the clause, which was written into the agreement by the former government.
I think the second question asked by the hon. gentleman may best be answered by drawing his attention to the final paragraph of the letter from the Japanese ambassador concerning the quantitative restrictions on exports of textiles to Canada. It reads:
In communicating this information to you, I assume that in respect of products listed in the annex to this letter, for which firm quantities are specified. Canada will not, during the year 1960, invoke the provisions of article XIX of the GATT or of the exchange of letters which accompanied the agreement of commerce of 1954 between Canada and Japan.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs is participating today in a meeting with representatives of the provinces. Notice of the question put by the hon. member for Laurier reached me just before coming into the house.

speechtext:
May I say that I am not aware on what information the statement to which the hon. member refers purports to be based, but I can assure him that in so far as the commonwealth scholarship program is concerned it is inaccurate to say that the universities of Laval and Montreal will not draw any scholarship holders who qualify for awards under this plan.
The plan provides for what are called inward and outward awards. Those offered by the government of Canada are inward, that is, for students from other commonwealth countries to come to Canada to pursue their studies. It is anticipated that in this category about 100 awards will be made this year and 200 in each of the subsequent years. I understand that from the applications already submitted for this type of award, through selection committees in other countries, a preliminary selection has already been made by the Canadian committee, and that it is quite probable that several of the successful candidates will pursue their studies at Laval, at the University of Montreal and also at the University of Ottawa.
In the case of inward awards, there are no payments made to Canadian universities except nominal amounts to cover actual administrative expenses. The scholar pays his own tuition fee from the amount of his grant.
With regard to outward scholarships, students from any university in Canada are eligible to apply, subject to the conditions agreed upon at the Oxford conference in the summer of 1959 and taking into account the 79951-0

Inquiries of the Ministry requirements of the governments of the countries offering the scholarships. These governments are responsible for deciding on the number of awards offered to Canadian students and for the payments to successful Canadian candidates. The final selection rests with those committees, but I am sure there is every reason to expect that candidates from the two universities mentioned by the hon. member are as likely to win awards as are candidates from other universities in Canada.

maintopic: REPORTED STATEMENTS ON APARTHEID BY PRIME MINISTER AND SOUTH AFRICAN REPRESENTATIVE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Leader of the Opposition put to me this question, as reported at page 3537 of Hansard:
I should like to ask whether he can resolve the apparent contradiction between the statement attributed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in London that he had made clear yesterday to Mr. Louw, the South African representative at the conference, the views of Canada with regard to apartheid, and the statement attributed to Mr. Louw today in reply to a question at a press conference that he did not hear the Canadian views from the Canadian Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, I was in telephone conversation with the Prime Minister last evening. He confirmed the newspaper reports that he had shortly after his arrival in London held a lengthy conference with Mr. Louw, at which he put before Mr. Louw very clearly and comprehensively the strong views entertained by the Canadian people and the Canadian government in reference to the policy of apartheid.
So far as the statement attributed to Mr. Louw in the press is concerned, I am informed that this press statement was drawn to the attention of Mr. Louw since it was raised in this house by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday afternoon. I am informed that Mr. Louw has stated that the statement attributed to him in the press was not correct, and that he simply said that it was not a matter for him to reveal what any other prime minister has said to him in conversation. I gather that the substance of what Mr. Louw had intended to convey in the statement he made to the press was that there had been no public discussion or any discussion at the formal meetings of the conference of prime ministers on the subject, but he did not intend to convey any suggestion that he had not been fully acquainted with or that he did not understand the views of Canada as a result of the talk with the Prime Minister of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a member of the socialist sector of the opposition I wish to address a question to the Minister of National Revenue. speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce concerning the surplus wheat agreement entered into by the United States and India yesterday. My question is this. Has the Canadian government, either through formal channels or informally, and either verbally or in writing, made any representations to the United States regarding this agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S. RESPECTING AGREEMENT WITH INDIA
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member's question might be answered by this summary of what has taken place.
In accordance with established procedures, both bilaterally with the United States and by the wheat utilization committee, we have been informed and consulted well in advance by the United States authorities regarding the P.L. 480 agreement with India which was concluded yesterday in Washington, D.C.
This agreement involves the supply of 3 million tons of U.S. wheat per year for four years to meet immediate consumption needs in India. In order to safeguard the commercial marketing interests of other wheat exporting countries, the Indian government has undertaken to purchase on commercial terms not less than 400,000 tons of wheat per year. This commercial quota is open to all wheat exporting countries, and is subject to review annually in the light of India's foreign exchange position. The agreement also provides for the supply of 1 million tons of U.S. wheat and 250,000 tons of U.S. rice per year for four years for a food reserve in India, details of which will be negotiated later in the light of the report of the wheat utilization committee mission to the Far East.
In view of the commercial quota of 400,000 tons, which represents a realistic assessment of what India's foreign exchange position will

Inquiries of the Ministry permit, and the fact that the arrangements for the supply of wheat and rice for the food reserve will take full account of the discussions at the next meeting of the wheat utilization committee, we feel that these provide ample safeguards for Canada's commercial interests. For these reasons we expressed no objection to the United States authorities in respect of this agreement, and indeed we extended our appreciation to them for giving us full and early opportunity for consultations.

maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S. RESPECTING AGREEMENT WITH INDIA
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Can the minister say whether the Canadian government has given any consideration to similar credit sales by Canada? Does not the minister believe that credit sales of this magnitude would go a long way toward clearing up Canada's wheat surplus?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S. RESPECTING AGREEMENT WITH INDIA
speechtext: Credit sales of this magnitude certainly would go a long way toward clearing up Canada's surplus position in wheat, but we are hardly able to conduct our affairs on the same basis as the United States, because we have not the same financial resources. However, in the past we have extended wheat to India on a loan basis. That was done in the years 1957 and 1958, and we have made substantial gifts of wheat and flour to the Colombo plan countries. On the basis of those gifts, rupees have been set up in what are called counterpart funds, and that money is then used by the local governments for improvements within their country.

maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S. RESPECTING AGREEMENT WITH INDIA
speechtext: I should like to ask a further supplementary question. Does the current deduction in Canada's credit sales or gifts of wheat to which the minister referred, as compared to 1957, indicate that Canada is abandoning what was a worth-while policy?

Mr. Speaker, a brief answer to the hon. member's question is that no legal suit has been taken against the commanding officer.
The problem of abandoned and derelict automobiles on service property is not a new one. In this case orders were promulgated in March and April that parking stickers would not be issued to cars not equipped with 1960 license plates. In early April a survey was made of the parking lots on the station, and a number of vehicles lacking 1960 license plates appeared to have been abandoned by their owners. On the 22nd April some 25 automobiles were removed, some to nearby service stations and others which were in very poor condition to the R.C.A.F. dump. While the dump is well posted, indicating that it is out of bounds to trespassers, unauthorized persons did gain entry and removed some parts of these vehicles. I understand the Ottawa city police are presently investigating.

Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock yesterday I was talking not so much about party doctrine -because I should like to emphasize that unlike my hon. friends alongside, the party which I support is not hidebound by doctrine -but rather was attempting to point out some principles which guide the party which I support in relation to the subject of dominion-provincial relations.
I pointed out the fact that one of the real reasons why a workable agreement has been brought about between the federal government and the provinces in relation to the subject before us today is that our party, in an atmosphere of good will, has produced an acceptable method. I pointed out that one of the principles our party has always adhered to since its inception, and one of the ideas it has always strongly upheld, is a high regard for local self-agency. I feel this should be emphasized, because I am now talking about the party principles which have guided, perhaps, the two major parties in our country since confederation.
I feel, moreover, that in normal times the Liberal party has adopted centralist principles which do not lend themselves to solving problems of this type. I am sure that today the Liberal party finds itself on the horns of a Hamlet type "to be or not to be" dilemma, and is confronted with a situation in which the Leader of the Opposition is prone to say, "on the one hand" or "on the other hand".
I know I will be accused of asking the traditional question, "How are you going to vote?" But I do ask my Liberal friends how they are going to vote on the bill. On the one hand they must realize that if they vote against it they will be depriving the universities of the province of Quebec of the moneys that will be granted to them under this legislation, and they know they will be voting against a workable method which has been brought about after consultation between this government and the various governments of the provinces. They know this is the case.
On the other hand I asked myself the question, "How are they possibly going to support this bill after days and days of talking
Dominion-Provincial Relations against so many principles which are inherent in it?" I am sure these questions have occurred to the Leader of the Opposition and the supporters who sit behind him, and I repeat that they find themselves on the horns of their traditional Hamlet type "to be or not to be" dilemma.
I now want to go further down the chamber and discuss the attitude of the C.C.F. toward this legislation. I have always known that even after having deserted most of their nationalization policies this party supports a degree of centralization which does not lend itself well to enhancing a good atmosphere in relation to dominion-provincial relations. But now we have another spokesman for the C.C.F., who made in this chamber not long ago what I can only term as one of the most unfortunate speeches to which I have listened since, as a young man, I entered the field of politics.
I ask the Leader of the C.C.F. today this question. When the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) spoke on this bill in this House of Commons, was he speaking for his party; or was he possibly speaking for the new party that-I hear an interruption from behind the curtain which is highly unparliamentary. I ask this question; it has to be answered. Will the leader of the C.C.F. party say that when the hon. member for Port Arthur spoke on this bill he was speaking as the spokesman for his party or for the new party they think they formed recently?
I reiterate, sir, that I know the hon. member, as he so often does, made a speech, and he hopes that some of us will give him the attention he wants. I have actually spoken to my confreres on both sides of the house, and a lot of them feel the silent treatment for him is the best thing, but I propose to give him and his speech a little attention.

I suppose this is what we might call good *"bull session" talk, but how ridiculous it sounded on the floor of this house. Now, sir, when I am talking about local pride and self-agency, I am talking about a principle in which the Conservative party believes. Mr. Speaker, as I am not an expert in constitutional law,
I had not intended to take part in this debate, but after listening to the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) I don't think anyone has to be much of a jurist to speak as he did.
His remarks were more in the nature of a tribute of appreciation to the provincial party responsible for his own election; they threw very little light on some points of the constitution.
University grants were established by the government at the request of the universities themselves and following the Massey commission report in 1950, because the universities were in financial difficulty. The St. Laurent government took action on the request at the time of the 1951-52 budget and at that time the house unanimously approved the measure.
In 1956 Mr. St. Laurent amended the act to provide that the funds would accumulate if some universities temporarily refused the grants.
That amendment, like the annual payments into the fund, was unanimously approved by the house. Thanks to the foresight of Mr. St. Laurent's administration, it is now possible for Quebec universities to recover those $25 million of which they have been deprived for the last eight years because of the malady which had been afflicting the leader of the Union Nationale, an autonomy obsession, as the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) said in Winnipeg.
Those university grants were not a mere whim on the part of the former Liberal government; for in the Massey report of 1950 we read the following:
The development of our country from every point of view is dependent upon our ensuring that through adequate training our ablest young people are equipped to carry out the tasks which they will be called upon to perform. Because of their financial circumstances, however, many of those potentially capable of playing an important role in the nation's development are unable, under present conditions, to get the necessary education. A national system of scholarships at all university

Dominion-Provincial Relations levels is therefore necessary in our country, and it must be founded upon adequate federal aid for the education of our ablest young men and women.
That same quotation may be found in the 1958 brief on government assistance to education.
First among those who recognized the practical measures designed to implement the recommendations of the Massey commission was Mr. St. Laurent himself, one of the public men most likely to inspire popular confidence, because of his obvious sincerity, of his dislike for opportunists and his recognized competence in constitutional law. Thus were grants distributed through the Canadian Universities Foundation to all universities of Canada during the fiscal year 1951-52.
But, afterwards, the Quebec Union Na-tionale government denied the universities the right to accept those grants offered through the conference, alleging that they were unconstitutional.
For eight years, the Union Nationale government took no apparent step or failed to submit any proposal to solve the problem, if problem there was. It is only on October 16, 1959, that Mr. Sauve, on behalf of the Quebec government, opened discussions with the federal government in order to come to an agreement and to recover the aforesaid $25 million, which has led to the bill now under review.
By virtue of this bill, Ottawa assumes the right to determine the amount of income a province may take out of a provincial tax levied for provincial purposes. Moreover, the federal government assumes as a matter of course the right to recover from equalization payments, any surplus yielded by the new provincial tax in lieu of federal university grants. Finally, the federal Minister of Finance reserves the right to decide whether arrangements made between provincial authorities and universities are satisfactory.
While speaking of the grant system introduced during the financial year 1951-52, the Solicitor General stated, and this is from page 3288 of Hansard for April 26:
-any legislation which finds its place in only nine provinces out of ten and is not acceptable to the tenth province leaves a very grave doubt as to its constitutionality.
Therefore, what the Solicitor General and his Tory friends from Quebec described at one time as unconstitutional must have become a matter admitting of no categorical


answer because he himself admits that it is a doubtful one.
If that is the case, why did the Quebec government, the Union Nationale and the Solicitor General fail to refer the matter to the supreme court? That would have been the best way to show they really meant to give financial assistance to universities.
It would be certainly interesting to hear the Solicitor General's reply to that question.
Incidentally, as I am not a lawyer, mine is only a layman's knowledge of the matter-

-and because of the Solicitor General's expressed doubt regarding the question of constitutionality, I would much rather approve the attitude of a man of recognized experience and ability, like the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent.
This legislation, designed to replace the former one, is a direct encroachment upon an exclusively provincial field by the federal government.
To use an expression preempted by the Union Nationale, I would say that, never since confederation, had a federal government had the audacity to invade in such direct fashion the administrative jurisdiction of a province.
Never has a federal government dictated to a province how it should spend its budget; yet such will be the result of this.
The federal government is telling the provinces to raise the income tax on corporations from 9 to 10 per cent and to spend the extra revenue on grants. However, if the yield of that tax exceeds $1.50 per capita, the said province is required under this act to hand over the balance to the federal government.
This Tory measure, I repeat, is direct interference in the administration of provincial affairs. And this is the kind of measure which has the approval of that so called autonomist, the Solicitor General, as evidenced by page 3287 of Hansard for April 26, 1960, where he said:
I am happy and proud, as a Conservative cabinet minister and as a member from Quebec, to be able to say we have contributed to this worthy cause by finding a solution to the problem of financial aid to universities.
That worthy cause referred to by the Solicitor General is an encroachment, a violation, and a backward step, to use the terms of Montreal's La Presse.
Refusing to betray the past of the Union Nationale, the Conservative members of the house prefer to betray the rights of the province.

To them, whether here or in Quebec, the only thing that counts is power, even at the cost of depriving some of our young people of a university education, when parents earn too little to pay tuition fees that are too high for most families in the working [DOT]classes.
Just to prove my point, let me refer to a table prepared in 1956 by the National Federation of Canadian University Students, on the basis of information contained in reports submitted to the Tremblay commission by Laval University, Montreal university and the Federation des Colleges classiques de la province de Quebec.
The most striking feature, in my opinion, is that 41.2 per cent-therefore almost half- of those students come from the wealthiest social classes which, in the province, form only 10.4 per cent of the working population.
In other words, the children of 89.6 per cent of the population have available for them only a little more than half the university capacity.
During the present debate, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreni-[DOT]ere) mentioned, as reported on page 9 of the appendix to Hansard for April 26, that during the period when the provincial government would not accept federal grants, universities had been treated generously since they had been receiving grants from the provincial government. And he went on to say:
To the figures I then mentioned I now wish to add that, since 1945, the Quebec government has paid to universities in my province the substantial amount of $112,036,297.38.
I do not challenge those figures given by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency; he will however not deny, I hope, that those provincial discretionary grants were derived from the taxes paid to the province by Quebec taxpayers.
Nor will he deny that, since the fiscal year 1951-52, the Quebec citizen has been paying a double tax for this purpose, that paid to the provincial government for university grants, and the one paid to the federal government for grants to universities of all the provinces, except Quebec.
Nor can he deny that, if Quebec had cooperated and made constructive suggestions, the amounts spent by the provincial government to replace the federal grants would have been used, over the last eight years, as

Dominion-Provincial Relations a provincial scholarships fund, so as to assist the sons of 89.6 per cent of the Quebec population made up for the most part of workers and farmers, who now account for barely more than half the university registrations.
It is not unfair to assume that, had it not been for the negative attitude of the Union Nationale government, many farmers' and workers' sons could have entered university through an altogether different policy of the Quebec government.
And I am not alone in thinking that the Quebec government's policy was one of no compromise.
I refer now to Hansard for April 13, 1959, at page 2649, to quote a statement made by the Conservative member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) about grants to universities:
That is why if the Quebec government cares to offer a suggestion, to make an official proposal, an appropriate and constructive one, I am positive that this government will consider it with great care and that, eventually, a decent solution will be found in this field.
This is hardly what the Union Nationale government has been doing for eight years.
They preferred to stick to their policy of no compromise; to ride their hobbyhorse of autonomy, a rickety one at that, by the Solicitor General's own admission, as far as the Liberal formula is concerned. However, I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that while this horse paid off plenty at the pari mutuel, in other words was of great help in winning provincial elections, it has handicapped a whole generation of workers' and farmers' sons who could have been helped by the province to the extent of the grants paid by their parents to the central government.
The universities themselves would have been only too happy, in view of their great need, to accept the grants established by the St. Laurent government.
Let me refer to Le Devoir for March 28, 1959 and read a few lines under the heading:
Federal grants must be recovered for Quebec universities
The University of Montreal alumni association and the federation of the Quebec junior boards of trade have again noisily taken up the moot question of education. Both groups call for immediate and positive steps to recover the substantial federal grants that universities and other educational institutions are unable to collect at the very time when their financial plight causes the deepest concern.
But, as was to be expected, Mr. Duplessis cold shoulders such initiatives and is not shy about deploring what he terms university "megalomania".

Dominion-Provincial Relations Two general solutions are suggested: (a) Alumni of the University of Montreal are planning to set up a federation, grouping graduates of all universities in the province, which would become, in Quebec, the counterpart of the Canadian Universities Foundation and could undertake the management and equitable distribution of federal grants, (b) The federation of junior boards of trade proposes, in its brief submitted to Mr. Duplessis, the setting up of a provincial commission on universities and colleges, which would be responsible for the fair distribution of federal and provincial grants.
The suggestions made at the time by those organizations are substantially the same, we have to admit, as those proposed by the Hon. Jean Lesage and the provincial Liberal party. The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) stated yesterday that the Hon. Jean Lesage was a new Duplessis.
In making such a statement the hon. member does not know that the Hon. Mr. Lesage was a member of the Liberal government which instituted those university grants, thus recognizing the needs of those institutions.
Nor, assuredly, has he taken a good look at the provisions of this bill, which constitutes a direct encroachment on the administration of provincial affairs.
Mr. Duplessis was denying universities the right to receive the grants entrusted by the federal government to the Canadian Universities Foundation which, itself, was handing them over to the universities, without any strings attached.
This bill allows for the payment of these grants providing the Minister of Finance controls the province and the amounts paid to the universities, and those are the very conditions which are unacceptable and Mr. Lesage is absolutely right in refusing them, as he expresses the public opinion prevailing in the province.
Going back to the same item of he Devoir which I quoted a while ago, I note that the universities were not always free to state their acceptance of the federal grants.
It is our purpose to act as a buffer, said Mr. Langlois. We want the universities dissociated from the provincial government and we want somehow to express what the universities are not free to say.
Facts show, added Mr. Tellier, that university authorities in Quebec are not willing to speak and whenever they do the opinion uttered is contrary to that expressed off the record.
Mr. Simon Langlois, whom I just quoted, was the second vice president of the Montreal university alumni association, and promotor of the plan is Mr. Claude Tellier.

Some Tory members from Quebec set themselves up as the true defenders of provincial autonomy, under the delusion that the Conservative government is the sole guardian of provincial autonomy.
That is why Mr. Andre Laurendeau wrote in he Devoir for September 9:
First of all, the Diefenbaker government, far from reversing its predecessors' policy, is giving it increased momentum: Canadian universities will receive an additional million from Ottawa ... The first startling fact is the attitude of the central government. During the elections, the Quebec partisans of Mr. Diefenbaker described him as a fierce autonomist. Well, what is he doing in the vital field of education? Precisely what Mr. St. Laurent had done after the Massey report. Consequently, the Quebec Conservatives voted in favour of legislation which had been partly promoted by the Rev. Father George H. Levesque, o.p., a former colleague of Mr. Massey's. What a strange turn of events-
The present legislation proves that the Conservatives want to encroach upon provincial administration, and it is revolting to see all Quebec Conservative members of the Duplessis school now oppose what they have preached in the past. They will vote for a formula of interference in the provincial field, whereas the one they criticized, though doubtful according to the Solicitor General seemed to us Liberals to have no strings attached and to involve no encroachment upon the academic field, since the federal government was making those grants through the Canadian Universities Foundation.
Conservative members from Quebec tried, as they are doing now, to praise the provincial government's action with regard to our people. Now, if we refer to a report by Mr. Paul Doyon published in October 1958, in he Devoir, we find that while those grants were being rejected for doubtful reasons, we were lagging behind the other provinces.
Further on, the article says that the University of Montreal received 36 per cent of its budget from the provincial government.
We can therefore see that the effort made by the Quebec government failed to equal the assistance received by universities in other provinces, because according to the same report, while, for instance, the University of Montreal was receiving 36 per cent of its budget in grants, universities in Ontario were getting 42.27 per cent, when federal assistance was added to provincial grants.
The people of Quebec will certainly realize that the position taken by the Union Nationale and by Ottawa Conservatives

always had and still has no other purpose than to make political capital at the expense of common sense.
So as to define exactly the Conservative position when they profess a genuine wish for autonomy, I should like to quote a few paragraphs from the writings of a public relations man for the Union Nationale and the Conservative party.
That man, a teller of tales about Quebec, said this when dealing with the Quebec Conservatives in a Montreal weekly dated April 30, 1960.
Never in our parliamentary history has the province of Quebec been so little defended by its federal members.
Never was such a weak delegation sent to Ottawa. It will be remembered that, even at the time of Bennett, the Quebec section of the Conservative party was pathetic. And little wonder, for what Quebec member of parliament, whether a minister, a parliamentary assistant or a private member, can boast of having achieved anything worth while?
About the cabinet ministers' lack of influence the item adds:
No, wonder, then, that French-Canadian members have no influence on the government. Prime Minister Diefenbaker has a solid background as a centralizer and an imperialist.
Concerning provincial autonomy the author has this to say:
As for the vital question of provincial autonomy, the Conservative government did not remedy any of the encroachments made by the Liberal government.
Of course, as a publicist for the Union Nationale, the writer is tearing into the Liberal party.
Yet in closing, he refers to the record of the Conservatives in Ottawa, and tells them they will not last out their five years.
The Conservatives are now adoring what they had been denouncing for ten years, and they are prepared to accept this unconstitutional formula and to support it with explanations that are rather lame, to say the least.
You, present Conservative members from Quebec, you, supporters of the Union Nationale, you are being inconsistent; you are bartering the rights of the province for a mess of potage.

The problem of federal assistance to Quebec universities is one which, for several years, has been causing concern among our French-speaking fellow citizens.

Mr. Speaker, the explanatory notes of Bill C-56 provide for alternative arrangements for the payment of grants either by Canada through the Canadian Universities Foundation, or directly by a province to institutions of higher learning, which grants are now paid under the Appropriation Act.
We know that the spirit of the 1953 act, passed by the Liberals, which defined the terms "university", "student", "university graduate", "university level", had not met with the approval of the universities, which since 1952 have been refusing any direct grants, because they rightly claimed that such a formula was a direct encroachment by the federal government on our system of education.
Mr. Speaker, the attitude of university leaders on this question was logical, unequivocal, clear and precise. But the Liberal government, disregarding their attitude, kept on claiming that university grants were constitutional, and by that very fact, kept on imposing upon the province of Quebec a system of grants which was repudiated not only by the government of the province of Quebec but also by the whole population, and on several occasions.
Since 1952, the Liberal government had been applying to Quebec universities the principle of "believe or die", by letting very

substantial amounts of money accumulate in the fund of the Canadian Universities Foundation, hoping thereby that some day our universities, being discouraged, would weaken to the point where we would make them accept that centralizing formula.
To be sure, the financial plight of our universities has been such that at one time the matter became a problem of cultural survival on a national scale. Our universities lacked the financial means of paying their professors the same rates of salaries as did universities in other provinces. That is why, for some years we were in the sad position where professors were leaving our Quebec universities to work in other more lucrative fields.
That situation, of course, could not go on indefinitely. In the last election campaign, Conservative members from the province of Quebec had promised the population that they would, with the co-operation of cabinet ministers, seek a more acceptable formula for our universities, one taking into account all cultural and racial factors of the problem, so as to prevent, on the national level, a discrimination which had lasted long enough. The sustained efforts and initiatives of Quebec premiers, implemented by their positive representations, and supported by the understanding of the present cabinet, finally produced results which for the moment are satisfactory and which, I repeat, were accepted by the population of the province of Quebec as a whole. Bill C-56 certainly contains certain imperfections; yet it is, to my mind, a constitutional recognition of the fact that education is an exclusively provincial field under section 93 of the British North America Act.
As we all know, the Quebec provincial government during the last session, passed some legislation to assist our universities, either by increased grants, or by underwriting loans to our universities by means of a consolidated fund, so as to further their development.
I think we should immediately establish a marked distinction by saying that the legislation now before us is not supplementary to other acts passed by the provinces with regard to education. Those are completely different provisions which are not mutually subordinate and they apply in altogether different fields.
In his speech of April 26, 1960, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier)
Dominion-Provincial Relations made much of the terms which were allegedly being imposed upon any province wishing to benefit under this legislation. Mr. Speaker, it requires a somewhat fertile and perhaps slightly deranged imagination to see in Bill C-56 facts that do not really exist. We should remember that this is fiscal legislation and that there is no question of a divided jurisdiction.
Now, where does it say in the act that, in order to exercise its jurisdiction on university education, a province must comply with any terms stipulated by this legislation? Clause 9A does not mention any. On the contrary, that section eliminates all terms imposed by the unamended part of the act or by various acts or procedures authorizing the Minister of Finance to decide who will receive grants awarded under the 1951 or 1954 formula. Nobody will find in clause 9A a single word which could lead to believe that the government of Quebec must obtain authorization from Ottawa to proceed with the direct financing of its universities.
On the contrary, we find that there is parallel action on the part of those governments. The first one, i.e. the government of Quebec, passes certain legislation guaranteeing exclusive action on its part with regard to the financing of education at the university level. Whether Bill C-56 is passed or not, it will in no way modify existing conditions in Quebec under the new provincial laws.
The object of this bill does not directly affect university financing. It merely concerns the deduction of certain taxes paid by Quebec corporations to the Quebec government and which are earmarked for university grants according to the province's own free choice.
The yield of the new tax, of which every Quebec corporation is exempt, is in no way limited by this legislation. Indeed, my colleague, the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Dorion), proved it the other day by indicating that Quebec universities will receive $1.75 per capita whereas the 1951 formula, amended in 1958, only provided for $1.50 per capita. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the present legislation authorizes a province to give more than $1.50 to its universities, if the province so desires.
All Bill C-56 does is to recognize given facts determined exclusively by the province. Instead of perpetuating a confusion which was created by the Liberals in 1951,

Dominion-Provincial Relations this government is offering every province the possibility of financing its university education directly by assigning to this purpose an additional 1 per cent of the corporation tax. Now, Mr. Speaker, what, exactly, is provided in the fiscal arrangements act? Any provincial income tax, or corporation or succession duties tax, will be subject to an exemption of so much per cent, according to the tax in question.
Bill C-56 exempts Quebec corporations of the whole additional 1 per cent which they will have to pay under freely imposed provincial legislation. It could just as easily have exempted that provincial tax up to the extent of $1.50 per capita only, or about 0.8 per cent.
In adjusting its equalization payments, either upwards or downwards, according to what the province will get, Bill C-56 follows exactly the same principle under which, in its other sections, it exempts provincial tax in a given proportion.
Unless the tax-sharing arrangements act is considered as absolutely unconstitutional, we must admit that the federal government has just as much right to adjust its equalization payment by setting a maximum amount as it can by a maximum deductibility percentage.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Laurier was the first one to give us an example of such procedure. I wonder if, like the hon. member for Laurier, we are not inclined to recognize as a debt to the federal government the equivalent of a provincial tax.
If it is fair and constitutional to deduct the income derived from the Quebec corporation tax from equalization payments due to Quebec, it is as fair and constitutional to deduct from those same equalization payments any amount levied by Quebec in addition to what the federal government is authorized, by statute, to earmark for university education.

Neither the parliament of Canada nor the legislature of any province can delegate one to the

Moreover, the provisions of the British North America Act contemplate these legislative bodies will, at all times, in the exercise of their sovereign jurisdiction, act as principals. In a word, Mr. Speaker, the conclusion is that the federal government cannot rent to the provinces its taxation rights, no more than the provinces can rent their own taxation fields to the federal government.

-but we offer an alternative, a realistic compromise allowing a province, such as the province of Quebec, to grant to its university population, the benefits which it was forced to refuse because of its scrupulous respect for the constitution and for autonomy.
Mr. Speaker, the others never referred to an unconstitutional legislation, they never challenged, nor requested the Quebec government to challenge in court the constitutionality of the 1951 act. They made speeches and said it was unconstitutional, but they never took the means to have it decided who was right and who was wrong.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, if we read again the Quebec resolutions, the Charlottetown resolutions and the London resolutions which preceded the signing of the confederation act, and I do not want to go further in this matter because the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) dealt with it, we see that the fathers of confederation never intended to seek a safeguard for anything else than primary education. Besides, the 1867 act says it has to do only with primary schools. Here is what we find at section 93 (2);
All the powers, privileges and duties at the union by law conferred and imposed in Upper Canada on the separate schools and school trustees of the queen's Homan Catholic subjects shall be-
In Canada, at the time of union, they talked about school trustees. Therefore, it is the schools that are under the responsibility of school boards, I mean the primary schools. Secondary schools were added just a few years ago.

But this does not cover classical colleges and seminaries, at all; they belong to the clergy-independently of the Quebec government-which has established its own curriculum and does not have to seek directives from the Catholic committee of the council of education to tell them what they should teach.
And the universities are independent universities, chartered by the government; they have a completely independent administration, and they too are autonomous. All those institutions are therefore independent, under the law and the constitution.
It is therefore clear that the intention of the fathers of confederation was to protect primary schools, which were under the direction of school boards. Again, that does not cover, in any way, shape or form, institutions of higher learning.

Mr. Speaker, before we adjourned at six o'clock, I was dealing with the views of the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) and, to my mind, his opinions rather come into direct conflict with those of the other cabinet members. For instance, I do not recall that since 1951 any minister of finance has, even once, maintained that university grants under the formula we established at that time were something irregular and anticonstitutional.
As a matter of fact, Mr. St. Laurent, who was a recognized authority on constitutional law, had studied the question and had come to the conclusion that those grants were not anti-constitutional.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I would rather accept the opinion of Mr. St. Laurent than that of the hon. Solicitor General. Indeed, I am not the only one to think so. All present ministers from the province of Quebec who have not spoken on the matter voted to maintain the same principle of university grants.
As I said before six o'clock, institutions of higher learning, such as the seminaries, which are owned by the clergy, the classical colleges and the chartered universities, do not ask the province which subject matters they should teach; and' they receive from the provincial government the grants necessary to

lessen education costs in our province. That is why it was thought necessary to offer those grants.
The confederation act-I am satisfied on that score and will remain so as long as it has not been proved otherwise beyond all doubt- aimed at protecting the schools under the school boards in order to safeguard the French minority in Quebec at that time.
I am not the only one to think so. Mr. Cyril James, a professional educator, who is remarkably conversant in that field, and is a scholar of repute, said, as reported in the French version of Hansard on pages 544 and 545, as follows:
There is no control of education, no infringement of provincial autonomy in the grants.
Neither the members of parliament who voted unanimously for the grant, nor the universities of Canada which were equally unanimous in accepting it, entertained the remotest idea that the federal grant carried any implications of control.
The possibility of any future danger to provincial rights is obviated by the presence of a provincial representative on the joint federal-provincial commission which administers the grants, it added.
Further down, he went on:
-"it has never been suggested that in making such gifts, the donors were legislating with respect to education"-
Similarly, while the Quebec government cannot legislate with regard to education in France, it none the less contributes generously to the Canadian students' house in Paris "and provides equally generous scholarships for students wishing to study in French universities."
Finally, he concluded:
"It is difficult to see how the legality of such federal grants can be questioned without similarly calling into question a wide variety of governmental practices, provincial as well as federal, which have been part of our accepted tradition for many years."
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, is it not a fact that the province of Quebec, which I congratulated at the time for this action, granted $50,000 to the University of Ottawa, and made other grants to the St. Boniface college and to a university in the maritime provinces? I say it was perfectly entitled to do so; it even had a duty to support French institutions outside the province. However, had permission first been sought from the government of the province to make these grants? No, that was not necessary.
Here is a statement by the Hon. Sidney Smith, the former president of the University of Toronto:

(Text):
Answering any argument that education is a provincial matter and therefore the federal government should keep out of it, he produced statistics which showed that 20 per cent of the 100,000 living alumni of the University of Toronto are in other provinces. The university is therefore making a national contribution. The same is true of all other Canadian universities.
(Translation):
Therefore, there are interchanges of students between universities, that is to say, there are young people coming from Ontario to Quebec, while others from Quebec go to Ontario, or from Quebec to the maritimes and from the maritimes to Quebec.
The fact is that the whole process is national in character, and the federal government was right in establishing the grants.
When one claims that something is irregular and illegal, one has to prove it. So I suggest to these people who claim that the grants as given under the Liberal formula were illegal, that they still have to prove it.
The thing to do, instead of trying to play politics with this, would have been for the Quebec government to go to the supreme court, which would have decided whether it was regular or irregular, constitutional or unconstitutional.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, it is not the first time that the Ottawa government has been giving grants.
I see here in a report presented by Mr. Enfield, a former member for York-Scarborough as recorded on page 157 of Hansard, that the amounts for education granted by the federal government in various provinces, in Quebec as well as in the other provinces,
were as follows:
British Columbia	 $2,989,000
Alberta	 2,261,000
Saskatchewan	 1,862,000
Manitoba	 1,437,000
Ontario	 7,228,000
Quebec	 2,952,000
New Brunswick, as well as all provinces, received grants and accepted them.
That is not something new either. Let us go back over the history of the grants made to the provinces:
In 1913 Sir Robert Borden gave $10 million to the agricultural schools.
In 1919 Sir Robert Borden gave $10 million to assist technical schools.
In 1939 the Right Hon. Mackenzie King had $4,500,000 voted as assistance to youth.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
In 1942 the dominion government voted $51 million under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act.
In 1951, $7,500,000 were voted as assistance to universities.
The province of Quebec accepted the grants and they were considered as constitutional.
The Solicitor General contends that they are anti-constitutional, but the Minister of Finance deems them constitutional.
Let me add that not one minister from Quebec tried to say that the subsidies granted under the Liberal formula were anti-constitutional.
The Solicitor General also had this to say concerning the bill before the house:
Its purpose is to render constitutional Liberal legislation on assistance to Quebec universities.
And in what way is it attempted to make this legislation constitutional?
Under the Liberal administration there was legislation providing for assistance without any strings attached. Universities were told: "Here are millions of dollars, you may do what you wish with them. This money is yours and you can use it as you see fit". There was no condition.
However, the very same people who refused millions from Ottawa accepted the millions of Mr. Rockefeller, accepted gladly all the millions coming from elsewhere, but the millions given by the Canadian government were refused. It was solely for the purpose of playings politics and the Solicitor General has attempted to play politics with this question of Quebec provincial autonomy that has never existed and does not exist with regard to university grants.
Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General is a lawyer. According to the Statutes of Canada, the Solicitor General is the assistant to the Minister of Justice, and when he made that statement, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) was absent. So, the Solicitor General was speaking as Minister of Justice when he said:
Mr. Speaker any legislation which finds its place in only nine provinces out of ten and is not acceptable to the tenth province leaves a very grave doubt as to its constitutionality.
Mr. Speaker, this legal pearl comes from a lawyer. I am not a lawyer, but when I hear such a statement coming from a lawyer, I wonder if the bar is very proud to have him as a member.

Mr. Speaker, the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) has criticized the principle of federal assistance. He said that the $25 million the Liberals had allowed to accumulate for the province of Quebec were a Tantalus cup which would force the universities to accept them.
Without the intervention of the federal government, the universities of the province of Quebec would still be hard up, and it is because Ottawa intervened to make grants to them that the government of the province of Quebec reconsidered its position and decided to do something to help them.
Mr. Speaker, according to the authorities of these institutions, it is Ottawa which is responsible for that and not the government of Quebec.
And when they talk of a Tantalus cup, what should we think of this attitude of Mr. Duplessis which led the heads of the universities to believe that if they accepted the federal government grants, they would not get any from the provincial government. Oh, Mr. Duplessis did not say it in those words. But it was quite clear, and the universities understood the attitude of the dictator and they refused the grants to please the ruler of the roost in the province of Quebec.
Will the Solicitor General ever understand that for many years the Quebec government has greatly hindered the development of our universities by preventing them, for political motives, not to say for motives of petty politics, to accept the grants offered to them by the federal government?
The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. English), I think, said that it was a fight between Ottawa and Quebec. That is not true. It was the fight of Quebec against Ottawa. That is all. It was the fight of the Union Nationale party against the Liberal party in Ottawa. And in support of my statement, you will note that since the Conservatives came into power in Ottawa, not one Quebec Conservative has dared criticize the policy of the federal Conservative government. Under the Liberal administration, everything the Liberals did was wrong; today, everything the Conservatives do is right because the Conservatives are in power.
Well, Mr. Speaker-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was saying that the hon. member for Hull denied the problem of autonomy when he said, among other things, that the problem has never existed and does not exist.
In that, he was only repeating the antiautonomist writings of Maurice Lamontagne, who just happens to be the official thinker of the Liberal party. May I add that it was a good thing to know, and that he should be heard outside the house. I understand, Mr. Speaker, that he has been heard in the past.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
However, the speech of the hon. member for Hull would have amused me right to the end had it not included such serious insults to the leaders of our universities in Quebec. They have just been accused of knuckling down to every political pressure by refusing federal grants to universities. The member for Hull ascribes to the rectors of our universities some shabby designs and some rather dark preoccupations. He thus insults His Excellency Msgr. Maurice Roy, chancellor of Laval University, as well as all our educators who, after deep reflection, decided to refuse the federal grants because, like former premier Duplessis, they saw in this measure a very dangerous precedent. These words will have to be recalled to the citizens of the province of Quebec, to all alumni of our universities who are justly proud of their alma mater and respectful of the men who taught them in the universities and who gave them, by their integrity, the best examples for their life. So, I want to protest now against the shameful remarks made by the member for Hull and deny categorically that our bishops, our rectors and our educators had surrended to lowly political pressure.
Mr. Speaker, when they started this debate on Bill C-56 and on grants to universities, the Liberals failed to mention the principles which inspire them and which have always led them in their centralizing endeavours.
Those principles, you have them set out on page 239 of the book by Maurice Lamontagne, Canadian Federalism, which, as everyone knows, is the bible of the centralizers.
Mr. Lamontagne wrote this:
At another level, one might wonder how long it will be possible to deny the federal government the right to play a part in the field of education and culture, when in fact it cannot help intervening.
Those are quite consequential premises which, unfortunately, are absolutely false, based as they are on a postulate which in fact begs the question.
Mr. Lamontagne starts by wondering about the part which the federal government would eventually be called upon to play in the field of education and culture. He seems to contend that the central government is bound to come into that field.
But at this point comes in the postulate on which is based' Mr. Lamontagne's argument.
Why is it, in the mind of the official thinker of the Liberal party, that one day the federal government will havea right to play a part in the field of education and culture.
Mr. Lamontagne answers straight off: it is because
-in fact it cannot help intervening.
[Mr Tremblay.]
The author of the breviary of centralization who may have some notion of what we call in legal terms the force of precedent, bases his whole argument on a de facto situation which he seems to consider as normal and taken for granted.
He gives examples, and I quote:
When a government has an exclusive jurisdiction on radio and television and must carry out its responsibilities in the field of the films, how can it be denied the right to concern itself with education and culture?
The illustration is rather badly chosen. Moreover, it concerns facts which will have to be reviewed sooner or later. For when the direct attacks by the central government on the exclusive rights of the provinces in the field of education are repealed once and for all, nothing will prevent the struggle to be continued in those sectors which were too quickly believed to be the responsibility of the central power.
In any case, to mention them in order to justify the federal government looking after the needs of our educational institutions, is to sidestep and try to confuse the issue, because one has not enough courage to face conditions as they are and to ask, as one should, the real questions: "Is the federal government entitled to look after education? And if that responsibility is not under its jurisdiction, why should it try to assume it?
That is how the problem should be put.
We know by now how the Liberal party answered those questions. After having stressed and solemnly stated that education was a provincial field, the spokesmen of that party then made some reservations, more particularly that universities are not within the traditional definition of education. That is a considerable limitation of the educational field and a refusal to admit that, in practice, universities are at the summit of a structure of which they are the ultimate perfect completion.
I would like to quote here part of a brief submitted by the University of Montreal to the Tremblay commission in 1954, which says:
We do not want any interference in the field of education, and we think that current university grants constitute such interference. In other words, we firmly believe-as we think that everybody else in the province of Quebec does too- that education is and must remain under provincial control and, that university teaching is part of the educational system; and we do not wish that system changed.
In drawing such a distinction between the various education and official academic levels, the Liberals were paving the way to greater encroachments.
But what is a university? Must we see in institutions of higher learning only technical

schools for the teaching of practical knowledge in specialized trades and professions? Must we give up the fine and great definition of universities, as understood by the ancients who considered it as the "mother of arts and science, and the source of all education"? Must we not consider any more the university as the ultimate level, the summit where education is being perfected? The Liberal contention knows no limit when it wants to deprive the universities of its basic role of co-ordinator in the field of education. What do those distinctions amount to which have been made between the various levels of education, primary, secondary and superior, if they are pot the various floors of a building whose summit is the university, both the summit and the foundation, because it is thanks to it that the education of an organized human community may go on improving and developing.
If help to universities is not help to education, universities must, from now on, be deprived of the role which they have never ceased to play as inspirators in all sectors of science, letters and arts, as a reference point and supreme master. One word only from the former member for Stormont today was sufficient to suppress the main function of universities, which is to preside over the manifold extension of knowledge which, added to directives and necessary guidance constitutes the traditional means of education.
But the Liberals have for long given up definitions. When definitions bother them, they ignore them and say they are not accepted as they used to be. That's what they did with the definition of education: they have restricted its scope at the primary level to justify the encroachment of the federal government upon the field of education because, in fact, assistance to universities, as it is practised today by the central government, covers both the university field proper and the secondary one, if we consider the structure of universities according to the American and Canadian pattern, according to which university begins at the senior matriculation level. And it is here that we realize the glaring ignorance or bad faith of those who state, like the former member for Stormont, that university grants are constitutional.
They ignore definitions as well as the facts they represent since, in this case, they deny the university its ordinary role and traditional function.
They conclude, with assurance, that assistance to universities is the responsibility of the federal government because it is not help to education. How simple it is.
