However, the truth is more complex. In the matter of grants to universities, the actions of the Liberals were not taken with such ease and facility. The thinkers on the payroll of the Liberal party had to put forward their greatest intellectual efforts to invent a formula designed to dress up in philosophical language the anti-constitutional manoeuvre of the Liberal party.
However, in referring to the subterfuges of the Massey commission, it is easy to see that the Liberals did not immediately find the elegant explanation given to us last year by that new Quebecer, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), to the effect that the Liberal party favours federal grants to universities because aid to universities is not aid to education. To reach that explanation, it was necessary to set up the now famous distinction between culture and education: and our self-styled philosophers finally settled the question by resorting to fine distinctions, with the help of a man who, though previously an unshakeable autonomist, compromised his "natural inclinations" once he became a royal commissioner, in favour of a thesis which was soon to be used by his political co-religionists to help the federal government meddle in the affairs of the provinces.
I immediately emphasize the contradiction into which the new convert from Laurier threw himself when he made the following statement last year, as recorded in Hansard for July 18, 1959. Having attempted to ascribe to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) an interpretation of the expression "grants to universities", the new Liberal messiah from Quebec expressed the view that the federal government should never consider financing education on the primary and secondary level. He made the following assertion with his usual solemnity when addressing his recently adopted province of Quebec, and I quote:
As far as I am concerned and I am sure not to be the only one on this side of the house to find myself in this position, I cannot accept that interpretation of federal grants to universities. I cannot accept that interpretation because it would justify federal assistance to secondary and primary schools. I want to make it very clear that X am and always will be strongly opposed to such federal grants.
I bear no grudge against the hon. member for publicly confessing today some feelings that he always managed, with infinite discretion, to keep for himself in the days when he lived outside the province of Quebec. However, I cannot believe he does not realize that the formula of grants to universities put forward by his party involves aid at the secondary level, because if you look at the American form of university organization, such as we find in English language Canadian

Dominion-Provincial Relations universities, you find that the university level starts at what corresponds to the matriculation grade for Canadian universities of European type. Thus, faculties of arts in American-type universities correspond, in our own universities, to the higher levels of the humanities. It is easily seen, therefore, that the argument in favour of grants to universities based on a definition of universities is unsound, because the type of university I have just referred to involves both the higher and secondary levels of education.
The former member for Stormont will forgive me if I emphasize the dilemma in which he placed himself. Either he knew nothing about the organization of Quebec universities and, in that case, he did not take essential precautions before voting with his government for legislation authorizing it not only to encroach upon the field of university education, but also the field of secondary education, because, as I have just stated, in American-type universities, students pursue studies which in the province of Quebec in particular, are made in college; or the hon. member was aware of this particular problem of university organization and deliberately accepted to take part in this huge quibble the sole purpose of which was to bring federal power into provincial affairs.

I believe there is a matter of language involved here. I did say, and I repeat, that it seems to me the hon. member for Laurier did not set out the problem as he should have; without crediting him with ulterior motive, I have the right, as a citizen, to wonder if this politician did really put the problem in the terms in which it should be put.
And, Mr. Speaker, if I may continue, I have said that we have every reason to believe that the Liberal members did not quite understand the problem of federal grants to universities. Under the Liberal concept, as evidenced by a speech to which I referred earlier, the hon. member for Laurier said, according to page 6374 of Hansard of July 18, 1959:
Since they were established in 1951, we have always said that such grants were constitutional.
Please note the force of the expression: "we have always said-" It should be added, Mr. Speaker, that he kept saying it despite the facts, despite history, despite the constitution and the experience acquired since even before the constitution, as was so ably demonstrated by my colleague for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion). What facts, what authors, what authority can the former member for Stormont and his co-religionists adduce in support of this claim? They initiated unconstitutional measures and, at the same time, they assumed that by crying out that they were right, this would justify them, in the eyes of the public, for violating the principles of the constitution for betraying history and plunging the Canadian confederation into a crisis which now, thanks to the Conservatives, seems to be abating. I have too much respect for the judgment of the Cornwall statesman to believe he relies on the whimsical explanation of the member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) who claimed, not so long ago, that university education was not under the jurisdiction of the provinces because there were no universities in 1867. He was quite wrong in saying so because Laval University, of which he is no doubt an alumnus, was founded in 1852, and because, no later than 1868, the Quebec government expressed its intention to take its responsibilities not only in the field of higher education, but in that of arts, science and humanities.
The first speech from the throne made at the first session of the legislature of the

province of Quebec included the following.
I refer to the Journals of the Quebec legislature, volume 1, pages 4 and 5:
The constitution has entrusted you with great interests and conferred upon you serious duties in the fields of justice, education, civil and municipal organization, public welfare, assistance to sciences, humanities and the arts, public development, including that of our vast forests and very important mines, in the fields of the development of our social resources, of immigration, of colonization, of police, and in general, in the fields of civil legislation and property rights.
And further on, the speech says:
The development of public education and the culture of science, literature and the arts have, in our times, become not only means of national progress and prosperity, but also, next to religious matters, the clearest manifestation of true civilization.
In that respect, the former province of Lower Canada has already made efforts which have been rewarded by remarkable success. So, with the commendable ambition of keeping us abreast of other nations, the former government had a survey made of the various educational systems used in Europe together with the literary and scientific institutions of the old world, with a view to introducing into ours what they might still be lacking. This is a serious matter which will soon have to retain the full attention of my government.
The budget speech of that year in the Quebec legislative assembly repeats just about the same thing. Let me quote from page 22 of the special edition of the budget speech delivered by the Hon. Mr. Dunkin on February 14, 1868:
A total of $392,190 is shown under the heading "Public Education". As 1 said before, about $25,000 of the total logically belongs to the civil government. And for the purpose of this statement that is where it was placed. I should point out that the balance includes three items, $68,000 for higher education, $4,000 for schools in the poorest municipalities and $2,000 for teachers' old age retirement fund, a total of $74,000 for the 12 months only, for those accounts are to be paid only once a year before the next meeting of the legislature. A new item of $12,000, about which I shall give more details later on, has been introduced for agricultural education.
There are under the same heading four literary and scientific institutions which receive a customary $3,000; then the usual amount of $2,000 is awarded to the commission on arts and manufactures; which makes a total of $5,000. The agricultural schools of Ste. Anne and l'Assomption receive $1,200 each; which brings grants for the whole agricultural field to a total of $14,400.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the centralizing undertaking of the Liberals in the field of education has known two stages:
1.	Introduction of university grant legislation;
2.	Creation of the Canada Council.
The two pieces of legislation could hardly be dissociated, as they are major links in a policy of centralization in the field of education which is, in itself, only one aspect of 79951-0-228J
Dominion-Provincial Relations the general centralizing policy described in Mr. Maurice Lamontagne's book which I mentioned earlier in my remarks.
I shall not recall here the various phases of the patient and astute struggle led by the federal government for the purpose of acquiring the exclusive provincial jurisdiction with regard to education. It might be enough to mention that the authors of the Tremblay commission report mentioned the milestones of that undertaking in book I, pages 95 and following, and in book II, page 227 and following, of that report.
I shall however more particularly mention the name of two members of the Massey commission, the same men whom Frangois-Albert Angers mentioned in his now famous article in VAction Nationale of November 1951, entitled:
Two models of irresponsibility: prime minister St. Laurent and commissioner Levesque.
The article mainly denounces the manoeuvres of those two men who were to become the great promoters of the centralization recommended, in matters educational, by the Massey-Levesque commission.
At the time the Liberal party was launching its great centralizing offensive some reasons and justifications had to be found. The views of the province of Quebec were too much feared in those days to state offhand as the new-Quebecer of Stormont did last year that university grants "were in accord with the constitution". They had to proceed with due caution. Pretexts and reasons had to be found which looked intellectual and even scientific.
A distinction was made between culture and education. It was to solve all difficulties and refute every objection. By resorting to that trick, everything which was in some way or other outside the questions specifically discussed in school programs was declared a cultural matter and therefore said to be under federal jurisdiction. Outside a specified zone which was called plain or academic education, a vast field was established, which was labelled the cultural field and comprised everything regarding the improvement of the individual and of society. Such a vast concept had to entail a very wide jurisdiction and what authority was better able to assume responsibility in this respect than the central power?
The concept of the university had to be redefined. Universities, because of the part

Dominion-Provincial Relations they played and because of their traditional functions, were supposed to belong to that super zone where central power may freely play.
After having disposed of the academic problem, it was also established that, for all practical purposes, the federal government should have a sovereign right of control with regard to all cultural matters and that such heavy responsibility could hardly be left only to provincial governments.
Therein, precisely, lies the misunderstanding, the error or the fraud. Those who were later on to become, in words if not in deeds, the promoters of a double culture, were forgetting that culture, according to the very definition they were giving of it, requires certain conditions and does not grow out of nothing.
In fact, it presupposes a certain climate, a certain environment. As a matter of fact, it is the result, the product and the most perfect achievement of a whole set of civilization factors.
Of these factors, the most important, the only essential one, is education. How can the advocates of dual culture claim to encourage the expansion and the progress of one culture in particular if they made this one culture subject to rules common to the two and if they seek, through a unified educational system, to cut off this culture from its living and fruitful sources?
Therein lies however the claim of the wise men from the Massey-Levesque commission. While pretending to promote a vaster form of national culture and to help spread French and English cultures, they want the central government to control these cultures and impose standards which, in the long run, would cause the original characteristics of each of these cultures to disappear.
What is, in fact, the objective advocated by the centralizing Liberals? The abolition of provincial sovereignty in matters of education and its transfer to a central power whose action could only be an effort towards levelling control of education at any level by the central power amounts to setting up a bureaucratic system which, to eliminate administrative difficulties, would impose programs that would do away with the destructive aspects of education in each province.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that every Canadian province must be anxious to retain full responsibility for education. Because education, and the system that serves to express distribute and expand it, is a provincial heritage enriched by experience gained over the years, and it illustrates the philosophy and distinctive characteristics of each province.
In the provinces with an English-speaking majority, even though the culture vehicle is


the same, that culture takes on the particular characteristics of the province, it reveals a background of tradition, customs and beliefs that perpuate the traditions, beliefs and national customs of those who built the province. Education, the responsibility for which belongs to each particular province, is a sure safeguard for the individual characteristics of every province. It thus goes on developing and enriching a body of traditional wealth, something which could not be done by a unified federal system of education.
What is true of education in provinces with an English-speaking majority is just as true, and even more, with regard to the province of Quebec and to the large French groups distributed across Canada. If French culture is to enjoy the greatest respect-as I am sure it does-as one of the most lively and dynamic cultures of the present day, there must also be a particular respect for the institutions that maintain and develop it in America, all the more so because that culture is an absolutely unique phenomenon in the North American context.
Canada would be all the poorer if French culture, which is one of its original features, should disappear. We have outlived the days when racial quarrels could be rekindled and where any excuse could be used to support the assimilation of one ethnic group by the other. Now is the time for a modus vivendi based on a respect for the facts of history and for the outcome of long political struggles.
It is proper to recall here the principles which guided the fathers of confederation when, after years of fierce and difficult struggles, they realized that both ethnic groups should try to find a modus vivendi whereby each respective group would have every opportunity to grow and develop freely.
Those principles were not discovered overnight; the light came only gradually, after a long search. And when Sir John A. Macdonald suggested a legislative union, it took all the persuasive powers of Georges-Etienne Cartier to convince him that such a form of union would not settle the old problems arising from the irreducible opposition between the two racial groups. Macdonald had to yield to the views of Georges-Etienne Cartier, just as today the Conservative government has yielded to the views of those who favour the strictest autonomy for the provinces.
There are those who will say that our government has not immediately settled the problem. That is true, but it started working on it as soon as it gained power. It sought

advice. It made suggestions. It listened to those that were made to it. It was able above all to learn from the facts and, instead of ignoring the province of Quebec, it started negotiations and agreed on a solution. The progress may have been difficult, I agree, but it was marked from the beginning with a persistent good will from which the whole country will now benefit.
This attitude stands in strange contrast with that of the Liberal party. It is useless to recall the heavy past of 1941, 1945, 1949, 1951 and the years preceding June 10, 1957.

I regret very much not being able to answer the question but I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker.
When I was briefly interrupted I was saying that the university grants, which were established by the St. Laurent government and which were accepted by the universities of Quebec from the joint commission of the federal and provincial governments in 1951 or in the fiscal year 1951-52, were not subsequently accepted by those universities after that commission was dissolved by the provincial government. For what reason that was done, I do not know. But from that time onward it was a source of regret to every member of the government of Canada, and to every member to whom I ever talked who supported the government of Canada of that day in this parliament, that a method could not be found of meeting this difficulty.
It is well known that in 1957 a step was taken by the government of that day, again on the initiative of Mr. St. Laurent, to have these grants paid not directly out of the treasury of Canada but by the national conference of Canadian universities or a foundation established by that national conference, in order to remove even the last faint vestige of the suggestion that there was any attempt, direct or indirect, to assert any kind of jurisdiction because these voluntary gifts were made by parliament.
When the equalization payments are accepted by the treasuries of the ten provinces or the nine provinces that accept them and that is every province that is offered them- the only one that does not get one is Ontario; and they are gratefully accepted by all treasuries now, especially by Quebec- I have never heard anyone argue that the provision of those equalization payments is an assertion by this parliament that we have control over the legislature of that province. I have never been able to understand-nor do I think have any of my hon. friends been able to do so-why anyone

Dominion-Provincial Relations should have any ground for the view that the payment to a free university in a free country of money voted by the parliament of Canada was anything more than a gift or that in any conceivable way it could exercise any jurisdiction over that university. I do not deny for one minute that such legislative jurisdiction as exists in this country over the universities is vested in the provincial legislatures and in them exclusively. But my idea of a university grant and the idea of every true liberal-and I am not using that word "liberal" with a capital "1"; I am using the word "liberal" with a small "1", the kind of liberalism that would be understood by the hon. member for Greenwood-is that a university should be free, that it should not be under the thumb of any government, federal, provincial or municipal. It was because no man ever respected the liberty or the rights of others in the whole history of this country more than did Louis St. Laurent that it was possible for him to do as he did.

I was going on to say that in 1957 when this new method of making the payments to the universities was adopted it was adopted not because of the situation in Ontario or in Prince Edward Island or indeed in any other of the nine provinces. It was adopted in the hope that this procedure might remove the difficulty or the susceptibility that was felt by many people-and honestly felt- in the province of Quebec. It is a susceptibility which is very understandable, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said this afternoon.
That is the kind of thing which, if we are realistic at all in trying to conduct the affairs of this country on a national basis with fairness to everyone, we have to pay due regard to. We were very disappointed indeed when that device did not have the result that was hoped for. I must say I was pleased, and I said so in the house when this measure was first brought before us by the Minister of Finance at the resolution stage. I said I was pleased, and I think everyone in the country who cares about these things at all was pleased that it appeared that a method had been found to overcome this susceptibility about federal aid to universities.
It so happens that when the bill was finally brought before us and we were able to examine the method by which the present government is seeking to do what Mr. St. Laurent sought by various devices to do

we found that there are very grave doubts indeed about whether it conforms with the constitution of Canada which it is our solemn duty in this house to uphold. We have no business to be making laws in this house which are beyond the powers of this parliament if we do so knowingly. When my hon. friend from Laurier, in that magnificent speech he made the other day, pointed out what the difficulties were, he was not for one minute suggesting, nor was anyone on this side of the house suggesting, that we do not want to see this problem solved. After all, these university grants were started by us and we want all the universities in Canada to have them. We are also glad that the Solicitor General is a convert to our view of this matter because he opposed these university grants rather mildly in 1957. He did not actually vote against them but he opposed them.
A good many hon. members who are supporters of our political opponents in the province of Quebec and who opposed us in the 1957 and 1958 elections also attacked these grants and said they would have an end of them when they came into this parliament. Now what have we here before us tonight? We have before us tonight a bill which continues absolutely literatim and verbatim the St. Laurent formula.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE

As a matter of fact we all know that that is the formula that is going to be followed in the case of nine provinces out of ten. So that when the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) says that is not true he evidently has not read the bill because the bill contains, as the Minister of Finance told us in his opening speech very categorically and correctly, a continuation of the existing formula of paying university grants. It also provides a suggested alternative which, in our opinion, is probably beyond the powers of this parliament validly to enact and which, whether it is beyond the powers of this parliament validly to enact or not, certainly interferes in provincial jurisdiction in several respects, and the St. Laurent formula which is also being continued by this bill interferes with it in no respect whatsoever. That is the difference.
What does this bill say? I am not going to read the clauses because the rules do not allow me, but in the general terms in which the minister explained it to us it says that the province could impose a tax of 1 per cent on corporation incomes in addition to the tax that it is now imposing, and that the federal tax will be abated by that 1 per cent if-
Dominion-Provincial Relations and it is the "if" that matters-the province pays to the universities grants equal to $1.50 per head according to a scheme that is laid down by an agreement between the Minister of Finance and the universities federation in which that province would not be participating. That is to say, the scheme that is to be followed by the province which accepts this alternative is a scheme that is laid down by an agreement between the Minister of Finance and representatives from the other provinces, but not from that particular province. It is imposed upon them.
Furthermore, it says that if more is collected from the 1 per cent levy than $1.50 per head of the population of the province, the excess has to be paid over to the government of Canada or will be deducted from the payments to the province under this act.
That is palpably and obviously an interference with the performance of the government, and indeed an interference with things which have been done by the legislature of the province. It is an interference laid down by this parliament to be carried out by the Minister of Finance. It makes the Minister of Finance a sort of university dictator in the province that accepts this alternative system. He lays down the rules for that province and that is what happens. That is why my friend, Mr. Lesage, who is the leader of a great political party in the province, has said it is not acceptable.
Members of the government say that they have solved the problem. They have not solved the problem as long as the new scheme is not acceptable to all the people any more than the old one appears to have been. So that the problem is not solved by this legislation even if it were valid, and it does seem to me that our first duty as legislators is to determine whether or not it is valid and to be thoroughly satisfied on that point. That is what we are paid for. That is what we are sent here for. That is our solemn duty in this parliament.
The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) made a speech yesterday and I had a lot of sympathy with what he said and I would like to recall one passage to hon. members. As reported at page 3559 of Hansard, he said:

I must say that was my first reaction when I heard of this entente. I think that was the first reaction of any person of good will,

speechtext:
With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, I will withdraw the word "nefarious" to replace it by the word "notorious".
I can understand the concern of Liberal members from Quebec who are sitting in this house and who have put their confidence in the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who, from time to time, appears on Quebec television-and, he is about the only one who does so-to preach the great Liberal doctrine which, according to him, is the only one able to solve all national problems, and especially to safeguard the autonomy of the provinces, particularly in matters of education.
I intend to speak very briefly about Bill C-56, and far be it from me to consider a legal text to analyse the constitutional implications of section 93 of the British North America Act.
I will simply put a few questions to the Liberal members of the official opposition, in order to judge, by their attitude, of their sincerity in discussing this bill.
Do the Liberals admit that education, at all levels, and under section 93 of the 1867 act, belongs exclusively to the provinces? Section 93 is quite clear on that point. Only the provinces are entitled to legislate in matters of education, which implies, therefore, that they have the exclusive right of levying funds to support schools and universities.
The hon. member for Laurier should give us an explanation of the policy adopted by his party when, on January 9, 1952, order in council P.C. No. 123 defined the terms "students" and "universities" for the purposes of implementing the federal act providing for assistance to universities.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
What was the definition given to the term "university level"?
As far as a province Is concerned, a program study stage more varied than that which is generally accepted in the provinces as entrance condition to university.
The situation became seriously endangered, and those conditions and terms forced the province of Quebec to refuse the federal grants.
In the province of Quebec, such encroachment on the part of the federal government on the field of education could not be accepted, because universities and affiliated classical colleges are their own masters with regard to their education program and enjoy the fullest autonomy. This freedom of action allows them to retain for our educational system its own distinctive character, which is so much in keeping with the traditions of the people of Quebec.
Considering that Canada has a dual culture, the French culture which is so rich, so beautiful and so noble and the Anglo-Saxon culture which is characterized by its beauty, dignity and richness; considering that educational programs and systems are based on either one or the other of those cultures, depending on the racial groups for which they were meant it was extremely dangerous for the preservation of the French fact, of the French language and of the French culture to agree that the definition of the words "student", "university" and "university level", as set out in order in council No. 123, be the same across the whole country.
It is then that we saw the late Hon. Maurice Duplessis, premier of the province of Quebec, take a strong stand. He fought aggressively for his people and the Almighty recalled him at the top of his glory September last, before he could even reap the profit of the great battles he fought against the centralization of the federal Liberal party, of which were members at the time the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and the ephemeral leader of the Quebec Liberal party, Mr. Jean Lesage, former member for Montmagny-L'lslet.
And it is those people who today, with regard to Bill C-56, talk about encroachment upon the autonomy of the province of Quebec. The former member for Montmagny-LTslet is very ill-advised to proclaim himself, in the province of Quebec, the champion of autonomy and education, because he supports today what he criticized formerly, and his sincerity is only equalled by a personal ambition dictated by the proud wish of becoming premier of his province.
There is many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip as Mr. Jean Lesage won't be long in finding out.


Liberal members of this house should put education before petty politics. We must first consider the problem of education if we want our young students, the citizens of tomorrow, to have all the educational facilities which will enable them to play their part in the political life of our country, a highly social part.
The Liberals believed and above all hoped that the Conservative government would fail to find an area of agreement, a solution acceptable to the province of Quebec. The matter of university grants is not definitely solved by the present bill, but it recognizes that the provinces have an absolute right to levy taxes for educational purposes and to be able to discharge the responsibilities devolved upon them by the constitution. The time for the gradual return to the provinces of their taxation fields has come and soon, the present government will give back to the provinces the privilege to exercise their exclusive jurisdiction as regards education and grants to education.
During the last federal elections, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) had promised a happy solution to the problem of university grants. The Canadian people and the people of Quebec have trusted him and today the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) by his bill is fulfilling this electoral promise.
I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the premier of the province of Quebec, the Hon. Antonio Barrette, for the strong stand he has taken in order to help our educational institutions and our universities in the province of Quebec. His government did not care to know what the federal government would do and, without knowing if Ottawa would accept the 1 per cent increase of the corporation tax for educational purposes, enacted a law whose constitutionality is recognized by Bill C-56 introduced by the Minister of Finance.
In order to avoid double taxation and to respect provincial autonomy, the federal government through Bill C-56 grants a deduction of 1 per cent on its own tax. Is that the breach of provincial autonomy mentioned by the member for Laurier and the exmember for Montmagny-LTslet? The latter would have done much more for his people had he taken the same stand which he advocates to-day when he was sitting in this house. What will be the attitude of the Liberals concerning Bill C-56? If they vote against the bill, we will come to the conclusion, (1) that they are opposed to the

integral maintenance of section 93 of the act of 1867; (2) that they blame the present government for being careful not to encroach upon provincial rights in the field of education; (3) that they blame the province of Quebec for recovering the sum of $25 million to assist higher education in Quebec; (4) that they prefer to help their little friend Jean Lesage than to serve the interests of education; (5) that they were and still are centralizers and continue to promote the "believe or die" or "take it or leave it" policy of the previous prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent; (6) that they have definitely no regard for provincial autonomy.
On the other hand, if they support Bill C-56, we shall conclude, (1) that they were not in earnest when they stated their argument on autonomy; (2), that they attempted to distract the people of Quebec in order to make them forget that the matter of university grants was settled through understanding, co-operation and absolute respect of provincial rights, between the Union Nationale government, on one hand, and the Conservative government, so efficiently headed by the Prime Minister, Mr. John Diefenbaker, on the other hand; (3), that they criticized this bill for five days for publicity purposes to finally approve it out of undue deference to public opinion.
In concluding, on behalf of the population of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere, I extend my heartiest congratulations to the Minister of Finance. And on behalf of educators, students, teaching institutions of my riding, I thank you, the Minister of Finance.
I shall support this bill and I vote for it, because it constitutes another step toward peace, harmony and true national unity in everyday life.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the debate on Bill C-56, which amends the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act.
According to pages 3279 and following of Hansard, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) made a complete historical survey of the matter of grants to universities, and his masterly speech covered the period from the request for financial assistance of Canadian universities to the Massey commission to the 1956 amendments which doubled those grants and charged the national conference of Canadian universities with their distribution.
I will briefly recall from this historical survey of the question only the essential facts.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
In 1950, and everybody knows this, the Canadian universities were in a disastrous financial situation-equivalent to a case of national urgency-which then required immediate solutions. We recall that in 1950, the universities themselves felt it was the duty of the government to help them.
So they explained their urgent needs to the Massey commission. The latter made a report on this matter to the federal government and urged it to revise the credits voted in aid to universities.
In the 1951-52 estimates, the special vote which provided direct grants to universities came from the consolidated revenue fund, not from a direct tax.
I must point out, Mr. Speaker, that those grants at the time were received with eagerness not only by all Canadian universities, but also by all political parties in the house, as well as by the government of the province of Quebec at the time, including the premier.
Those grants to universities initiated in 1951-52 either were constitutional or not.
If they were unconstitutional, why then were they approved without restriction by all political parties, by all provincial governments, including the Union Nationale and Mr. Duplessis?
If, on the other hand, the direct grants to universities were constitutional in 1951 and 1952, according to the Union Nationale and Mr. Duplessis, why did they become unconstitutional for them in later years?
We are all free to draw our own conclusions. My opinion is that in 1952 and 1956, which were election years in the province of Quebec, the Quebec government at the time deemed it expedient to entertain a constitutional myth for purely political purposes, feeling it was much more advantageous to use those expedients than solve the problem of the Canadian universities.
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative members of the province of Quebec were elected, among other reasons, because of formal promises they made to the electors in that province. Our Conservative friends undertook, if elected, to find a formula by which no federal grant would be paid to universities. And now Bill C-56 is before this house.
Not long ago I was reading thoughts by Euripides and I remember this Latin quotation which, I think, applies to this case: Quos Deus vult perdere prius dementat.
Those whom God wishes to destroy He first deprives of their senses.

Business of the House
Mr. Speaker, the bill under consideration is in two parts, one of which is basically wrong, dangerous and anti-constitutional. That part is precisely that which is known as the Diefenbaker section.
On the other hand, there is in Bill C-56 a part that is good, and it is precisely the part taken from the act passed by the Liberal government of Mr. St. Laurent.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask you to call it ten o'clock?

speechtext:
Room 701, Metcalfe building, 88 Metcalfe street,
Ottawa 4, Ontario, Canada,
April 29, 1960.
The Honourable Donald M. Fleming,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
As you well know, careful consultations have been going on between the two of us, as well as between the staff of the Canadian departments concerned and my embassy, as to the size of quota to be voluntarily applied by Japan for export to Canada of commodities which might injure or threaten to injure the Canadian producers of such or like products.
I am happy to inform you that as a result of these consultations, my government has decided to apply voluntary export quotas on textile goods as set forth in the annex to this letter for the year 1960.
You are aware that in addition, the Japanese government also maintains voluntary export control on other secondary textile products. These are listed in the final page of the annex. In respect of these items it is the intention of the Japanese government to establish export quotas for the year 1960 which provide for a moderate and orderly expansion on the basis of 1959 shipments.
It is noted that these measures, as set forth in the annex, are taken by the Japanese government on its own accord in order to conform with its established policy of gradual increase of Japanese exports on an orderly basis with a view to avoiding undue injury to the domestic industry of importing countries.
You will also note from the annex that many new items have been included under control and almost all items, at least all important items, of the secondary textile goods-nearly 100 per cent of the total Japanese export to Canada of garments or 77 per cent of secondary textile goods-will be covered by these measures. It is the opinion of my government that these controls will effectively preclude any further flooding in any of these categories of goods.
I take this opportunity to renew my firm belief that by setting up these self-restraining measures, we have been able to pave the
way for the further expansion of two-way trade on an orderly basis, to the mutual benefit of both countries.
In communicating this information to you, I assume that in respect of products listed in the annex to this letter, for which firm quantities are specified, Canada will not, during the year 1960, invoke the provisions of article XIX of the GATT or of the exchange of letters which accompanied the agreement of commerce of 1954 between Canada and Japan.
Yours sincerely,
Toru Hagiwara, Ambassador of Japan.
